content.content:
# ARCHITECTURE.md — Katalyst

> The technical counterpart to `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md`. That document says what the tool must do and why; this one says how the system is shaped, where each rule is enforced, and how it runs. It describes the system **as built and as planned**, and each section says which.

**Living document.** Last verified: 2026-09-17. Any pull request that changes a boundary, a layer, a data flow, or a runtime dependency updates this file in the same PR. A stale architecture doc is worse than none: it is the "not knowing why it did that" failure in written form.

**Status markers.** `[planned]` — decided, not yet in the repo. `[built]` — in the repo and covered by the tests named. `[stretch]` — designed for, not scheduled.

---

## 1. The system in one picture `[built]`

Both halves of the drawing below run today; the event stream, the model pipeline, the grounding adapters and the stored state are decided but unwritten, and are named again under it.

```
 ┌──────────────────────────── browser ─────────────────────────────┐
 │  React + TypeScript (Vite)                                       │
 │  workbench canvas · inspector · world-state strip · thesis dock  │
 └───────────────▲───────────────────────────────▲──────────────────┘
        HTTP JSON │                               │ server-sent events
                  │                               │ (one-way stream: proposals,
                  ▼                               │  rejections, propagation)
 ┌──────────────────────────── backend ─────────────────────────────┐
 │  FastAPI (Python web framework)                                  │
 │                                                                  │
 │  api/        routes, request/response shapes, the event stream   │
 │  engine/     talks to the model; turns answers into proposals    │
 │  domain/     PURE: graph rules, propagation, branches. No I/O.   │
 │  grounding/  adapters for outside data (Polymarket, FRED)        │
 │  settings.py the only place environment variables are read       │
 │                                                                  │
 │  storage: one SQLite file on a volume (sessions, branches,       │
 │           generation transcripts)                                │
 └──────┬──────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬───────────┘
        ▼                      ▼                        ▼
   Anthropic API         Polymarket Gamma API        FRED API
   (claude-opus-5,       (prediction-market          (economic series,
    web search tool)      prices, no key)             free key)
```

**What runs, and what is drawn ahead.** The browser app and the Python server both start, and `api/` answers three things for real: whether the server is up, what it calls itself, and the stored worked example. `domain/` holds the rules and nothing else. `[planned]` Four parts of the drawing have no code behind them. There is no event stream — every route today is an ordinary request and its answer. `engine/` holds identifier minting alone; nothing has ever called Anthropic's API. `grounding/` is an empty package; nothing has ever called Polymarket or FRED. There is no storage: no database file, no volume declared in either compose file, nothing kept between requests. Inside the browser box only a status screen exists; the canvas, the inspector, the world-state strip and the thesis dock are drawn because they are decided, not because they are written.

Two halves, one contract: the backend publishes an OpenAPI description (a machine-readable list of every route and data shape); the frontend's TypeScript types are generated from it and committed, and continuous integration fails if regeneration would change them. The two halves cannot drift silently.

---

## 2. The one rule that shapes everything `[built]`

Half of this is mechanical today: the boundary that keeps the rules layer pure is checked on every pull request, and `validate` already refuses a bad map. The other half — a recorded model answer carrying a loop, refused by that same validator — waits for stack 04, because nothing calls a model yet.

**The model proposes; the domain layer disposes.**

The language model never edits the graph. It returns *proposals* — one proposition or one link per call — and code the team wrote checks each proposal against the rules of the graph. A proposal is accepted (and gets a server-minted identifier) or rejected with a reason. Both outcomes are events on the stream, so the user sees the model's misses as well as its hits.

This is why `domain/` is pure: no network, no model, no clock, no randomness except an explicit seed. It is the part of the system whose correctness is *proven by tests* rather than *requested of a model*, and it is the part a reviewer should read first.

Enforced by `test_domain_imports_nothing_impure`, in `backend/tests/unit/test_import_boundary.py`: it reads every file under `domain/` and fails if one of them imports `engine/`, `api/`, `grounding/`, or a model client. It runs in the `backend` check on every pull request, and two further tests in the same file check the checker itself, so a boundary test that has quietly stopped looking cannot pass by accident. The same checker is pointed the other way by `test_the_rules_layer_never_reads_the_examples`, so whether a map is valid can never come to depend on which worked examples we ship.

The disposing half exists too: `validate` in `domain/validity.py` walks a whole map and returns every fault at once, each named in the claim's own words rather than by identifier. `[planned]` The recorded test — the model returns a graph with a loop and the validator rejects it — arrives with stack 04.

=== §7 ===
## 7. Testing layers `[built]`

## 1. The system in one picture `[built]`

**What runs, and what is drawn ahead.** The browser app and the Python server both start, and `api/` answers three things for real: whether the server is up, what it calls itself, and the stored worked example. `domain/` holds the rules and nothing else. `[planned]` Four parts of the drawing have no code behind them. Inside the browser box only a status screen exists; the canvas, the inspector, the world-state strip and the thesis dock are drawn because they are decided, not because they are written.

## 2. The one rule that shapes everything `[built]`

Half of this is mechanical today: the boundary that keeps the rules layer pure is checked on every pull request, and `validate` already refuses a bad map. The other half — a recorded model answer carrying a loop, refused by that same validator — waits for stack 04, because nothing calls a model yet.

**The model proposes; the domain layer disposes.**

The language model never edits the graph. It returns *proposals* — one proposition or one link per call — and code the team wrote checks each proposal against the rules of the graph. A proposal is accepted (and gets a server-minted identifier) or rejected with a reason. Both outcomes are events on the stream, so the user sees the model's misses as well as its hits.

This is why `domain/` is pure: no network, no model, no clock, no randomness except an explicit seed. It is the part of the system whose correctness is *proven by tests* rather than *requested of a model*, and it is the part a reviewer should read first.

Enforced by `test_domain_imports_nothing_impure`, in `backend/tests/unit/test_import_boundary.py`: it reads every file under `domain/` and fails if one of them imports `engine/`, `api/`, `grounding/`, or a model client. It runs in the `backend` check on every pull request, and two further tests in the same file check the checker itself, so a boundary test that has quietly stopped looking cannot pass by accident. The same checker is pointed the other way by `test_the_rules_layer_never_reads_the_examples`, so whether a map is valid can never come to depend on which worked examples we ship.

The disposing half exists too: `validate` in `domain/validity.py` walks a whole map and returns every fault at once, each named in the claim's own words rather than by identifier. `[planned]` The recorded test — the model returns a graph with a loop and the validator rejects it — arrives with stack 04.

1	/**
2	 * The second world: the base map with a branch folded onto it, as far as
3	 * structure goes and not one step further.
4	 *
5	 * **What this builds is real, and what it leaves out is left out on purpose.**
6	 * Applying a branch properly means running the map's numbers again, and that is
7	 * the engine's work. This half of the product does none of it. So the world
8	 * below carries everything the branch says about *shape* — which claim arrived,
9	 * which arrows came with it, which arrows a supposition cut, which claims the
10	 * edit can reach and which it provably cannot — and, wherever a likelihood would
11	 * have moved, **an absence with its reason** rather than the old number left
12	 * lying there looking current.
13	 *
14	 * That is the honest half and it is the useful half: *here is what your edit can
15	 * reach, and here is what it cannot* is this product's central correctness claim
16	 * made visible, and it needs no arithmetic at all.
17	 *
18	 * Three rules hold it together:
19	 *
20	 * 1. **A claim your edit can reach shows its model number's absence.** The
21	 *    number on the base map is the base map's number; on this branch it would be
22	 *    something else, and nothing has worked out what. Leaving the old one on
23	 *    screen would be the quietest lie in the product.
24	 * 2. **A claim your edit provably cannot reach keeps its number, unhedged.**
25	 *    That is not optimism: an edit reaches only what is still joined to its
26	 *    subject, and everything else is identical.
27	 * 3. **Your own number is yours.** *My own number* writes into your own slot and
28	 *    is never averaged with the model's or a market's, and it is not pushed
29	 *    through the map — so it fills in immediately and moves nothing else.
30	 */
31	
32	import type { Absence, BranchView, ClaimView, LinkView, Slot, WorldView } from "../../world/types";
33	import { badgesByClaim, standingByClaim } from "./badges";
34	import { readDiff } from "./diffState";
35	import type { Arrow } from "./reach";
36	
37	/**
38	 * What stands where a likelihood would go on a claim this edit can reach.
39	 *
40	 * The words are the shared vocabulary's; the sentence says which number is
41	 * missing and who would have to work it out.
42	 */
43	export const NO_ENGINE: Absence = {
44	  kind: "no_engine",
45	  words: "no engine yet",
46	  reason:
47	    "Nothing has worked this number through the map yet. Your edit can reach this claim, so " +
48	    "its likelihood would move — and the part of this product that works out where to is not " +
49	    "connected. The old number would be the base map's, not this branch's.",
50	};
51	
52	/** That slot, ready to be dropped into a claim. */
53	const NO_ENGINE_SLOT: Slot = { absence: NO_ENGINE };
54	
55	/** Every arrow, as working out what an edit reaches needs it. */
56	function asArrows(links: readonly LinkView[]): Arrow[] {
57	  return links.map((link) => ({
58	    id: link.id,
59	    source: link.source,
60	    target: link.target,
61	    reflexive: link.reflexive,
62	  }));
63	}
64	
65	/**
66	 * Fold a branch onto a base world and hand back the second world.
67	 *
68	 * Both worlds are drawn in one coordinate space afterwards, so nothing here
69	 * moves a claim: the union of the two maps is laid out once and painted twice.
70	 *
71	 * @param base The base world, exactly as the map was written.

1	/**
2	 * The world source that reads the stored example the server ships with.
3	 *
4	 * Everything the canvas draws in this build comes through here, from
5	 * `GET /api/fixtures/hormuz`. Not one claim, likelihood, arrow or date is typed
6	 * into the browser. If the server's copy of the example changes, the picture
7	 * changes with it and nothing here needs editing.
8	 *
9	 * **What the numbers are, said plainly.** The stored example's likelihoods were
10	 * written by hand, and the file that holds them says so in its own comments:
11	 * they are illustrative, so the machinery has something honest-shaped to run
12	 * on. They are not computed and this half of the product computes nothing. The
13	 * sentence in `origin` below is what the screen prints under the map, so a
14	 * reader never has to take that on trust.
15	 *
16	 * There is no arithmetic in this file. A likelihood is read from the server and
17	 * carried, untouched and at full precision, to the component that prints it.
18	 */
19	
20	import { readExample } from "../api/client";
21	import type { components } from "../api/schema";
22	import type { FixtureBundle, WorldSource } from "./source";
23	import type {
24	  Absence,
25	  AbsenceKind,
26	  BaseRateView,
27	  BranchHue,
28	  BranchView,
29	  ClaimView,
30	  Edit,
31	  EvidenceClipping,
32	  LinkView,
33	  Slot,
34	  SourceView,
35	  WorldRequest,
36	  WorldView,
37	} from "./types";
38	
39	type Proposition = components["schemas"]["Proposition"];
40	type Belief = components["schemas"]["Belief"];
41	type Evidence = components["schemas"]["Evidence"];
42	type Source = components["schemas"]["Source"];
43	type Branch = components["schemas"]["Branch"];
44	type Graph = components["schemas"]["Graph"];
45	
46	/**
47	 * Turn a likelihood from the server into a filled slot, unchanged.
48	 *
49	 * The three numbers are copied across at full precision. Rounding is a display
50	 * decision and is made once, in the chip that prints them.
51	 */
52	function filled(belief: Belief): Slot {
53	  return { reading: { p: belief.p, lo: belief.lo, hi: belief.hi } };
54	}
55	
56	/** Turn "there is no number here" into the words and the reason for them. */
57	function missing(kind: AbsenceKind, words: string, reason: string): Slot {
58	  const absence: Absence = { kind, words, reason };
59	  return { absence };
60	}
61	
62	/**
63	 * The single letter that stands for a publication, taken from the host name in
64	 * its own web address.
65	 *
66	 * `https://www.bbc.com/news/...` gives `B`. A leading `www.` is dropped first,
67	 * because every publication has one and it would make every monogram a `W`.
68	 *
69	 * A letter rather than the publication's own icon, deliberately: an icon is a
70	 * request to somebody else's server, and this app draws its first frame without
71	 * making one.
72	 */
73	export function monogramFor(url: string): { monogram: string; host: string } {
74	  let host: string;
75	  try {
76	    host = new URL(url).hostname;
77	  } catch {
78	    // An address we cannot read is not a crash. The clipping still has a line
79	    // to show, and the mark beside it says plainly that there is no host name.
80	    return { monogram: "?", host: "an address we could not read" };
81	  }
82	  const withoutWww = host.startsWith("www.") ? host.slice(4) : host;
83	  const first = withoutWww.slice(0, 1).toUpperCase();
84	  return { monogram: first === "" ? "?" : first, host: withoutWww };
85	}
86	
87	/** Turn one published item into the clipping a tile shows. */
88	function clipping(evidence: Evidence): EvidenceClipping {
89	  const { monogram, host } = monogramFor(evidence.url);
90	  return {
91	    line: evidence.claim,
92	    monogram,

cd /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst-wt/feat-03b-diff && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
feat(canvas): two worlds in one picture, the six buttons, and the whole keyboard

Two maps now exist the moment you edit one, and the screen answers the
question that matters: what did my edit reach, and what did it provably
leave alone. The union of both is laid out once and painted twice in the
same coordinates, so every difference you see is a real difference and
not a re-layout.

Four states, all worked out from the branch and none of them from a
number: the claim your edit added, a claim you supposed false, a claim
your edit can reach, and one it cannot. On the strike branch OPEC+'s
announcement comes out untouched, because the only wire that could carry
the edit to it is the feedback arrow, and feedback arrows are set aside
when the question is what can move.

Where a likelihood would have moved there is an absence with its reason.
Nothing here computes a number, and the branch's buttons build a branch
and show it rather than moving one.

Also: the rail of endings the edit can reach, in map order and ranked by
nothing; the six buttons word for word from the vocabulary; the branch
panel as a sequence; j/k down a column and h/l along the wires with a
line under the map naming the wire it took; the map as a list; and the
one animation on the map — wires arriving column by column, which keeps
its ordering when the operating system asks for less movement.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -20
